::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Today's Big Question"}
**Across a dozen cases, what have we actually learned about who holds power over global business — and how it can be held accountable?**

# The arc {background-color="#990000"}

## Where we've been

- **Module 1 — Scene-setting:** firms as global and political actors; why countries want FDI in
- **Module 2 — Political risk:** Aceh, Siemens, ISDS and Philip Morris
- **Module 3 — Accountability:** tax (Apple), advocacy & self-regulation (Patagonia), tariffs & sourcing (LeapFive), apparel labor (H&M)
- **Module 4 — Geoeconomics:** CFIUS/TikTok, culture (Fuyao/*American Factory*), forced labor (UFLPA)

# Throughlines {background-color="#990000"}

## The tools we used again and again

- **Power, authority, autonomy** — who can make whom do what
- **Collective-action problems** (the prisoner's dilemma) — corruption, tax competition, labor standards
- **Public vs. private regulation** — and the **right to regulate**
- **The obsolescing bargain** and **weaponized interdependence**

## One organizing question

Almost every case came back to: **where does power sit in this relationship, and what — if anything — can hold it accountable?**

# The big debates {background-color="#990000"}

## Revisited

- Is global business, on balance, a **net positive**? Who gains and who loses?
- Can firms **self-regulate**, or is public regulation essential?
- When does **economics become security** — and what does that cost?

You don't have to land in the same place I do. You do have to **reason from evidence**, the way every case write-up asked you to.

# Final exam {background-color="#990000"}

## What to expect

- **Cumulative**, covering the concepts, cases, and discussions across all four modules
- Review materials posted on **Canvas**; bring questions to office hours
- During finals week (Dec 14–18) — day and time per the registrar

## Thank you

It's been a pleasure thinking through these cases with you this semester.
